video_title: Bond Yields On The Spectrum: From Good To Ugly (with special guest Nick Raich)
gist: Ed Yardeni lays out four scenarios for rising bond yields, from good to ugly: growth and a higher neutral rate (his base case for the US), the oil war shock, the yen carry trade, and a Dalio-style debt crisis (with France as a flashpoint). He flags the hawkish pivot under Fed chair Warsh and widening credit spreads. Guest Nick Raich (Earnings Scout) says S&P 500 estimate revisions are decelerating much as in 2021; he still sees higher prices through year-end but warns that a second weak revision quarter would open an 'alligator jaw' and signal de-risking and a tech underweight ahead of a possibly ugly 2027.

themes.theme: Bond yield spectrum: good to ugly

insights.claim: Yardeni frames the rise in bond yields along a four-scenario spectrum: better-than-expected growth (good), the war/oil shock (transitory), the yen carry trade unwinding (global), and a Dalio-style debt crisis (ugly), possibly in combination.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Use the four drivers to diagnose each leg of the yield move rather than assuming one cause.

insights.claim: Yardeni attributes the rise in US yields mainly to better-than-expected growth, while the globally synchronized rise in yields is better explained by the yen carry trade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: US yield upside is a growth repricing, not a fiscal panic, per Yardeni; global yields carry Japan-driven contagion risk.

insights.claim: The neutral interest rate is likely higher than the Fed thought, because growth is increasingly driven by productivity, consumers are resilient, AI capex is strong, the government is borrowing about $2 trillion in capital markets, and retiring baby boomers are dissaving.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Structural demand for credit argues against a return to low rates.

insights.claim: Yardeni rejects 'higher for longer' in favor of 'normal for longer', arguing yields are simply repricing back to the old normal of a healthy economy.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Do not expect a reversion to post-GFC low yields.
insights.quote: it's not higher for longer, it's normal for longer

insights.claim: Yardeni's bond-vigilante test: with nominal GDP growing about 6.5% y/y and the 10-year below 5.5%, vigilantes are not yet at work; they would be 'working overtime' only if the 10-year yield rose above nominal GDP growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Watch the 10-year vs nominal GDP growth gap as the trigger for the ugly scenario.
insights.quote: I'd be telling you the bond vigilantes are working overtime if I saw the 10-year yield rising above nominal GDP GDP growth.

insights.claim: Even in a debt-crisis scenario, Yardeni expects Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to pull out the 'bazooka' by buying back far more Treasury bonds and issuing more bills, limiting the damage versus Ray Dalio's doom scenario.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A Treasury policy put on long yields caps the tail risk of a disorderly bond selloff.

insights.claim: Oil shipments through or around the Strait of Hormuz are reportedly back to about 95% of pre-war levels, yet oil prices remain sticky; Yardeni assumes oil will flow and higher output from Canada, the US and Venezuela will bring prices down.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Falling oil would relieve one of the four yield-pressure drivers.

insights.claim: France is showing signs of a looming debt crisis that reminds Yardeni of Greece around 2010, when bond vigilantes drove Greek yields sharply higher.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: French spreads are the place to watch for a sovereign-debt flare-up in Europe.

insights.claim: Credit spreads widening in investment grade and high yield, following CCC spreads and higher CDS prices, are worrisome to Yardeni, because the credit market is where trouble usually starts when the Fed is hiking.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Credit is the early-warning gauge for something breaking in this tightening round.
insights.quote: credit markets is always where the the the trouble trouble start

insights.claim: The Fed pivoted from seeing policy as modestly restrictive at the start of 2026 to hiking: under new chair Kevin Warsh (from June) it held in June and July with three dissenters wanting hikes, then raised 25bp unanimously in September.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Markets now debate whether hikes come in October and December or only December.

insights.claim: Warsh described the September hike as removing a dose of accommodation, which implies the Fed sees the funds rate as still below neutral and has more to do.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Signals further tightening rather than a one-and-done hike.

insights.claim: Yardeni calls this a second round of tightening, arguing the Fed erred by cutting 175bp in 2024-2025 (the bond market agreed, since yields rose instead of falling) and is now correcting with at least two hikes.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Expect at least two hikes in total; the earlier easing is being unwound.

insights.claim: Yardeni projects S&P 500 forward earnings rising from $419 to $425 by year-end, and is not troubled by the flattening 2027 consensus.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Top-down earnings still support equities through year-end.

insights.claim: 2026 S&P 500 earnings are distorted by mark-to-market gains on hyperscaler stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic (Amazon in Anthropic, Google in SpaceX), so the market is focusing on 2027 estimates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Strip out investment gains; 2027 forward estimates are what drive valuation.

insights.claim: Excluding mark-to-market gains, Q2 2026 S&P 500 earnings grew 26% versus a normal 6-8%, with a 37% beat rate, and second-half outlooks were raised; the market is up 13% YTD, 22% since March 30, and 116% since the bull market began.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Peak growth sets up tougher comparisons and deceleration in 2027.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 multiple compressed from 22x last year to 18x this year, which Raich reads as the market rationally paying less for expected earnings deceleration and Fed tightening, so it may be cheaper for a reason.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: A lower P/E is not a value signal when the expected E is about to slow.
insights.quote: it might be cheaper for a reason

insights.claim: Yardeni moved Tech and Communication Services from overweight to market weight at the end of last year for diversification, since together they make up about 45% of the S&P 500; his old rule is that a sector reaching 33% usually marks its top.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Concentration risk alone argues against overweighting mega-cap tech.

insights.claim: Raich's 'alligator jaw' signal triggers when the rate of change in S&P 500 estimate revisions weakens for two or more quarters while price keeps rising; it has preceded every major correction and bear market seven times in 35 years.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: A second weak revision quarter alongside new highs would be the de-risking trigger.

insights.claim: S&P 500 estimates rose 3.2% after Q1 2026 earnings season but only 1.96% after Q2, so revisions are still positive but decelerating, giving a one-quarter divergence so far.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Q3 2026 earnings season decides whether the jaw opens.

insights.claim: Raich says 2026 revision trends are almost identical to 2021, not 2000: in 2021 revisions went from +5.1% to +3.38%, then were flat in Q3, the jaw opened, and it closed with the 23% bear market of 2022 that bottomed October 12, 2022.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Use 2021-2022 as a roadmap: a strong 2026 followed by possible bear-market risk in 2027.
insights.quote: 2026 from an estimate revision standpoint is more like 2021. It's almost identical.

insights.claim: Among the 16 early August-quarter reporters, Micron has the best revision trend at +8% but it is cooling from earlier quarters, and the group's estimates are rising 1% versus 11% six months ago.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Early reporters suggest Q3 revisions will weaken again, pointing toward a jaw.

insights.claim: Raich contrasts last year's setup (Fed cutting while revisions and growth accelerated) with today's (Fed hiking, rates rising, 2027 growth set to decelerate, revisions weakening), and warns that 2027 could be ugly.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Macro and micro both turn less supportive into 2027.

insights.claim: Raich still forecasts higher stock prices through year-end, arguing that bull markets die on euphoria rather than with a whimper, so a blow-off top in tech is likely before the jaw closes.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Stay long for now; the de-risking point comes after a euphoric leg.
insights.quote: bull markets die on euphoria. They don't die with a whimper

insights.claim: When the jaw opens, Raich will recommend underweighting tech, because high-beta names sell off the most; he turned less bullish on tech in August but remains bullish for now.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Tech underweight is the first move once the signal triggers.

insights.claim: Raich argues that sell-side consensus already embeds secular trends and company guidance, so measuring the change (delta) in consensus is a cleaner gauge of business momentum than second-guessing the levels; companies mostly revise estimates only four times a year after they report.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Track revision deltas around reporting seasons, not absolute estimates.

insights.claim: A 10-year yield of 5.32% does not scare Raich as long as earnings expectations keep improving; falling oil and yields that revive revisions would push the 'hurricane' off course.
insights.speaker: Nick Raich
insights.so_what: Earnings revisions, not yield levels, determine his equity stance.
